orig_text:
The presence of the SSRC in the EKTPlaintext ensures that an attacker
   cannot substitute an EKTCiphertext from one SRTP stream into another
   SRTP stream.  This mitigates the impact of cut-and-paste attacks that
   arise due to the lack of a cryptographic binding between the EKT Tag
   and the rest of the SRTP packet.  SRTP tags can only be cut-and-
   pasted within the stream of packets sent by a given RTP endpoint; an
   attacker cannot "cross the streams" and use an EKT Tag from one SSRC
   to reset the key for another SSRC.  The Epoch field in the
   FullEKTField also prevents an attacker from rolling back to a
   previous key.
correct_text:
The presence of the SSRC in the EKTPlaintext ensures that an attacker
   cannot substitute an EKTCiphertext from one SRTP stream into another
   SRTP stream.  This mitigates the impact of cut-and-paste attacks that
   arise due to the lack of a cryptographic binding between the EKT Tag
   and the rest of the SRTP packet.  SRTP tags can only be cut-and-
   pasted within the stream of packets sent by a given RTP endpoint; an
   attacker cannot "cross the streams" and use an EKT Tag from one SSRC
   to reset the key for another SSRC.

   Because the Epoch field in the FullEKTField is outside EKTCiphertext
   and is not integrity-protected by the EKT Cipher (Section 4.1,
   Section 4.4, and Section 4.4.2) or by the SRTP authentication tag
   (Section 4 and Section 4.3.1), the Epoch field alone does NOT
   prevent an attacker from rolling back to a previous key: an on-path
   attacker holding a previously captured FullEKTField (and an
   authentic SRTP packet under that previous key) can rewrite the
   cleartext Epoch field to a value higher than the highest epoch seen
   by the recipient, satisfying Section 4.1's monotonicity rule.  This
   also allows an attacker to inject an artificially high Epoch (e.g.,
   0xFFFF) to cause denial of service against subsequent legitimate
   rekeying under the same SPI.  Section 4.1's Epoch check therefore
   prevents only unmodified replay of older FullEKTField values and
   non-increasing Epoch values.  To bound rollback and epoch-exhaustion
   exposure without changing the wire format, implementations MUST check
   Epoch monotonicity during inbound processing (Section 4.3.2),
   SHOULD reject implausibly large Epoch jumps relative to the expected
   key-rotation schedule, and SHOULD rotate EKTKey (via DTLS-SRTP)
   before Epoch approaches exhaustion or whenever rollback/DoS is
   detected.
notes:
Methodology & Tooling Disclosure:
I am not claiming personal expertise at the level of formal protocol verification; this submission was heavily assisted by Google Gemini alongside my open-source RFC-LLM pipeline (https://github.com/mariobx/RFC-LLM) and MITRE CPSA 4.4.9 (`cpsa4`). All RFC quotes were verified verbatim against the published .txt specification, and the formal counterexample witnesses were produced mechanically by `cpsa4`, submitted in good faith for WG / Area Director review.


Section 6 currently states unconditionally: "The Epoch field in the FullEKTField also prevents an attacker from rolling back to a previous key." This claim is contradicted by the wire format and cipher specification in RFC 8870 itself:

1. Unauthenticated placement of Epoch (Section 4.1):
   FullEKTField = EKTCiphertext SPI Epoch EKTMsgLength EKTMsgTypeFull,
   whereas EKTPlaintext = SRTPMasterKeyLength SRTPMasterKey SSRC ROC.
   Only EKTPlaintext is encrypted/wrapped into EKTCiphertext. Epoch sits
   in cleartext outside EKTCiphertext.

2. Placement outside SRTP authentication (Section 4 and Section 4.3.1):
   The EKTField appears *after* the SRTP authentication tag, so SRTP
   authentication does not cover Epoch, SPI, EKTMsgLength, or
   EKTMsgTypeFull.

3. No AAD or metadata binding in EKT Ciphers (Section 4.4 and Section 4.4.2):
   AES Key Wrap (AESKW) wraps EKTPlaintext with no Associated
   Authenticated Data, and Section 4.4.2 specifies that EKT Ciphers
   "SHOULD NOT use other EKT or SRTP fields as an input."

4. Inbound Processing (Section 4.3.2):
   Section 4.3.2 step 4 parses EKTPlaintext as described in Section 4.1,
   but does not explicitly restate Section 4.1's Epoch rejection check
   when processing inbound FullEKTField values before installing the
   SRTP master key.

Because Epoch is unauthenticated, an attacker who records an earlier FullEKTField (containing EKTCiphertext for an old SRTPMasterKey, e.g., at Epoch = 0) together with a previously authenticated SRTP packet (or who targets pre-SRTP-tag EKT processing per Section 4.3.2) can overwrite the cleartext Epoch bytes to any higher value (e.g., Epoch' = current + 1 or 0xFFFF). The receiver's Section 4.1 check ("reject any future FullEKTField for this SPI and SSRC that has an epoch value equal to or lower than an epoch already seen") will accept the modified packet, permitting both key rollback to the captured earlier key and permanent Epoch-exhaustion DoS for that SPI/SSRC.

Formal Verification Evidence:
Automated cryptographic protocol analysis using MITRE CPSA 4.4.9 (cpsa4) finds, in a model of RFC 8870 written by the pipeline from the RFC text (ekt_dtls_srtp.scm / ekt_dtls_srtp_shapes.txt, realized shape label 8), a PARAMETER_DISAGREEMENT_DETECTED outcome under uncompromised EKTKey: an authentic receiver accepts a FullEKTField whose cleartext epoch, ekt_spi, and ekt_msg_length differ from the sender's transmitted values (epoch != epoch-0, ekt_spi != ekt_spi-0, ekt_msg_length != ekt_msg_length-0) while recovering the wrapped EKTPlaintext. This is a result about the model, not a machine-checked proof about RFC 8870 itself.

Supporting model artifacts:
- CPSA model:
  https://github.com/mariobx/Errata-for-RFC-Editor/blob/main/RFC8870/ekt_dtls_srtp.scm
- Non-shapes XHTML output:
  https://github.com/mariobx/Errata-for-RFC-Editor/blob/main/RFC8870/ekt_dtls_srtp.xhtml
- Shapes XHTML output:
  https://github.com/mariobx/Errata-for-RFC-Editor/blob/main/RFC8870/ekt_dtls_srtp_shapes.xhtml

Scope Note per IESG Errata Processing Guidelines (May 2021):
Changing EKTPlaintext (e.g., moving Epoch into EKTPlaintext alongside SSRC and ROC) or switching the EKT Cipher to an AEAD mode taking (SPI, Epoch, EKTMsgLength, EKTMsgTypeFull) as AAD alters the wire protocol and cannot be done in an erratum. The Corrected Text removes the false security guarantee in Section 6 and specifies wire-compatible defensive guidance, while documenting the cryptographic binding fix as an issue for a future -bis revision (Hold for Document Update if normative rekey/Epoch-jump heuristics exceed erratum scope).
